\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Retrieval over visually rich documents.} Document question answering was long built on OCR text, and
benchmarks such as DocVQA~\cite{docvqa}, InfographicVQA~\cite{infovqa} and multi-page DocVQA~\cite{mpdocvqa} showed
how much of the answer lives in layout, tables and graphics. Retrievers that embed page images directly avoid the OCR
step: DSE~\cite{dse} encodes a document screenshot into one vector, and ColPali~\cite{colpali} keeps a vector per
image patch and scores queries by late interaction~\cite{colbert}. VisRAG~\cite{visrag} and M3DocRAG~\cite{m3docrag}
feed retrieved page images to a vision-language generator, and OHRBench~\cite{ocrhinders} measures how OCR errors
propagate through text-based RAG. These systems fix one context modality for every query. We keep both and ask, per
query, whether the image, the OCR text or both are worth their cost, measured end to end with one generator.

\paragraph{Adaptive retrieval and model routing.} Several methods decide per query how much retrieval to do.
Mallen et al.~\cite{mallen} retrieve only for questions about less popular entities, FLARE~\cite{flare} retrieves again when the
generator is unsure of upcoming tokens, Self-RAG~\cite{selfrag} trains the generator to emit retrieval and critique
tokens, and Adaptive-RAG~\cite{adaptiverag} classifies question complexity to choose between no, single-step and
multi-step retrieval. A parallel line routes queries between language models of different size and price:
FrugalGPT~\cite{frugalgpt} cascades models with a learned answer scorer, Hybrid LLM~\cite{hybridllm} and
RouteLLM~\cite{routellm} train routers whose threshold sets the cost--quality trade-off at run time,
AutoMix~\cite{automix} escalates after the small model verifies its own answer, and RouterBench~\cite{routerbench}
compares such routers on cached outputs. CAVR shares the run-time cost weight and the cached-output evaluation with
this work, but routes between context modalities for one generator, so the cost difference comes from input
processing rather than model size, and it predicts quality from what retrieval returned before any generation.

\paragraph{Efficient late-interaction and vector search.} Late interaction stores many vectors per item.
ColBERTv2~\cite{colbertv2} compresses them with residual quantisation, PLAID~\cite{plaid} prunes candidates with
centroid interaction, MUVERA~\cite{muvera} reduces multi-vector search to single-vector search with fixed-dimensional
encodings, and token pooling~\cite{tokenpooling} clusters each item's vectors and keeps the cluster means, which we
evaluate on our page index. For single-vector search, FAISS~\cite{faiss} runs billion-scale nearest-neighbour search on
GPUs and DiskANN~\cite{diskann} serves graph indexes from solid-state drives on one node. We measure the simplest exact baseline,
exhaustive MaxSim, sharded across GPUs or streamed from host memory, so that the placement costs are explicit; these
engines are complementary and would lower the retrieval tier we project.

\paragraph{Inference serving.} Serving systems batch and schedule requests to meet latency targets on shared
accelerators: Clipper~\cite{clipper} adapts batch sizes per model, Clockwork~\cite{clockwork} makes latency
predictable by controlling execution, INFaaS~\cite{infaas} picks model variants per request to meet accuracy, latency and
cost targets, and AlpaServe~\cite{alpaserve} multiplexes models across GPUs with model parallelism. For generative
models, Orca~\cite{orca} schedules at iteration level, vLLM~\cite{vllm} manages the key-value cache in pages,
DistServe~\cite{distserve} and Splitwise~\cite{splitwise} place the prefill and decode phases on separate GPUs, and
SGLang~\cite{sglang} reuses shared prompt prefixes. These systems make each request cheaper or better scheduled; CAVR
reduces the work a request asks for in the first place. Because our answers are short, the cost is dominated by
prefill over the retrieved context, which is the phase that routing shrinks.
